opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what excites me most is that we're finally seeing a genuinely different way of generating text that actually works at scale. For years, the assumption has been that language has to be produced autoregressively — one token at a time, left to right — and that's how essentially every large language model works today. But that's a very sequential process, and it puts a hard ceiling on how fast you can generate, no matter how much hardware you throw at it.

Diffusion models take a different approach. Instead of committing to each word one after another, you start from a rough, noisy version of the whole output and refine it in parallel over a number of steps. That's the same basic idea that made diffusion so successful for images, video, and audio, and a lot of my academic work over the years has been on the foundations of those models. What we've shown at Inception is that you can bring that coarse-to-fine generation to language and code and get quality that's competitive with strong autoregressive models, while being several times faster and cheaper to serve, because you're making much better use of the GPU.

And speed isn't just a nice-to-have. When generation becomes that fast and that cheap, it changes what you can build: real-time coding assistants, voice agents that respond naturally, agentic workflows that make many calls in a loop without users waiting around. There are also some interesting qualitative advantages. Because the model can revise any part of the output during generation rather than being locked into earlier choices, it has a natural ability to correct itself, and it's well suited to things like infilling and editing, where you care about context on both sides.

So for me it's that combination: a new foundational approach, grounded in years of research, that's now practical enough to deploy and could really reshape the cost and latency curve of AI applications.

r001.rationale: The response applies diffusion to language and code, but does not mention DNA as discrete data.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes faster generation and names real-time coding assistants and voice agents that respond naturally, conveying suitability for latency-sensitive applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. What excites me most is that diffusion gives us a fundamentally different way to generate text, and I think it breaks a tradeoff that the whole field has just accepted as inevitable.

Every large language model people use today is autoregressive. It produces one token, then the next, then the next, strictly left to right. That means latency scales with the length of the output, and no matter how much hardware you throw at it, you're bottlenecked by that sequential loop. Diffusion models work the other way around. You start from noise, or a rough, fully masked draft of the whole sequence, and then you refine all of it in parallel over a handful of steps. So instead of generating a thousand tokens in a thousand passes, you can get there in something like ten or twenty. That's where the speed comes from, and in practice we're seeing something on the order of five to ten times faster generation on the same GPUs, which also translates directly into cost.

But honestly, speed is the headline, not the thing I find most interesting. What I find more exciting is what this does to the quality of reasoning. Autoregressive models can't take back a token once they've emitted it. If they commit to something wrong early in the sequence, they have to live with it. A diffusion model sees the whole draft and gets to revise it. It can fix an error in the middle after it has figured out how the end should look. That's much closer to how people actually write or solve problems. We produce a rough version and then iterate. I think that opens the door to much better controllability and much fewer of those hallucinations where a model paints itself into a corner.

The other piece is that this is the same paradigm that transformed image and video generation. Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, Sora are all diffusion models. Text was the one modality where that revolution hadn't happened yet, mostly because discrete tokens are harder to apply the math to. A lot of my academic work at Stanford was on exactly that problem, how to make diffusion work on discrete data. At Inception we've been able to turn that into models that are competitive with the leading autoregressive systems on quality while being dramatically faster. Seeing that go from a research idea to something that actually works at scale is the part that keeps me up at night in a good way.

r001.rationale: The response discusses applying diffusion to text and notes that discrete tokens make the math harder, but it does not mention code or DNA as discrete data.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes faster generation and lower latency, but does not identify applications with very tight latency budgets as a particularly suitable use case.

astra-6.text:
What excites me most is the opportunity to rethink how we generate language. With an autoregressive model, you produce one token at a time, from left to right. Each step depends on the previous one, so there’s a fundamental sequential bottleneck.

With diffusion, you can work on many parts of a sequence in parallel and refine them together. That opens up the possibility of much faster generation, but also a different way of composing an answer. You can start with a rough version and revise it, rather than committing to every word before you’ve generated what comes next.

At Inception, what’s exciting is taking that idea and making it practically useful. Can we deliver strong language capabilities while improving speed and computational efficiency? That combination could make a real difference for applications where latency matters. And scientifically, I think there’s a lot left to explore about what this different approach to generation makes possible.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me most is the opportunity to rethink how we generate language. With an autoregressive model, you commit to one token at a time, from left to right. With diffusion, you can work on multiple parts of a response in parallel and refine them together.

That opens up some really interesting possibilities. One is speed: how much more efficiently can we generate high-quality text? Another is flexibility. If you’re writing code or filling in a document, you often have constraints coming from both before and after the piece you want to generate. An approach that can look at the whole thing and iteratively improve it feels very natural for those tasks.

Of course, you have to make that work in practice—parallel generation only helps if the refinement process is efficient and the quality is there. But that’s what makes it exciting. There’s a lot of room to explore a different way of building language models.
